paras: The expulsion of a labor agent near Pulaski, Tennessee, took place in early 1881, when a mob drove away a man who had recruited about forty Black laborers to move to Jackson County, Arkansas. The laborers reached Jackson County, and the mob was described as opposed to "the negroes leaving that section." The episode is known from a single brief in an Arkansas newspaper.

According to the Sharp County Record, "forty-odd negro laborers" had recently been brought to Jackson County, Arkansas, from the vicinity of Pulaski, Tennessee. They had come at the urging of a man who "went after and induced them to come," whose name and race the paper did not give.

The same item reported that this recruiter was driven away from the Pulaski area by a mob. The paper gave the mob's motive as opposition to the Black laborers leaving that part of Tennessee, but it gave no date, place, size of the mob or names. No injury to the recruiter or to the laborers is reported.
No report of arrests or of any official response appears in the coverage.

The only account appeared on March 10, 1881, in the Sharp County Record (Arkansas), as one sentence in a column of news grouped by county. Under the heading "Jackson," it ran between a note on a Newport livery man who ran a skiff during wet weather and the obituary of a Jacksonport lawyer. The paper offered no comment on the mob, treating the arrival of the laborers as local news, and no Tennessee report of the expulsion appears in the coverage.
